source.title: Revenge of Monosemanticity: Neuron Specialization as a New Form of Feature Learning in MLPs
source.authors: Amirhesam Abedsoltan; Enric Boix-Adserà; Fivos Kalogiannis; M. Belkin

page_placements.theme: Units mix features without capacity pressure

record.tranche_reason: The study measures neuron activation concentration across known synthetic clusters, using a different measure and setting from the cited interpretability work. This bears conceptually on activation-based monosemanticity and its variation across activation architectures.
record.gate_note: The experiments use synthetic clustered regression tasks, not image classifiers, language models, or semantic examples such as cat faces and cars. The rows record the study's activation-based monosemanticity measurements across activation types. The study's specialization-alignment percentages are not included as rows because weight alignment alone does not measure the versions' semantic behavior. Predictive-MSE comparisons are also not included because they do not measure monosemanticity.
record.test_reason: In synthetic clustered-regression MLPs, the study reports how many weight-specialized neurons fire mainly on one cluster, for four activation functions. Cluster selectivity is a toy analogue of monosemanticity, so this is a new-setting result on V5. The measure covers only specialized neurons (Sj ≥ 0.9), not all neurons, so it is an indirect proxy for the share of polysemantic neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that MLPs on clustered data develop neurons specialized to single clusters, and that a substantial fraction of these fire mainly on their cluster. Specialization does not guarantee monosemanticity. They call the monosemanticity finding 'consistent across activations' and stress activation differences mainly for sample complexity (gated activations better). They do not frame monosemanticity as varying by activation. They also prove specialization (Theorem 1) and an MLP-versus-RFM sample-complexity separation (Theorem 2).
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic clustered regression, geometric alignment to known cluster-specific subspaces, and activation-energy concentration by cluster; it does not use the original interpretability methods or natural semantic stimuli.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured monosemanticity differs across activation types (ReLU, GELU, ReGLU, SwiGLU) and across the reported single-index and multi-index experiment settings.

fits_no_version.finding: With width 4096 far exceeding K = 25–50 clusters, many weight-specialized neurons still spread activation energy across clusters. Examples: GELU has only 45.7% of specialized neurons with Mj > 1/2 (axis-aligned setting), and SwiGLU 56.7% (multi-index). Mean Mj is about 0.44–0.67 for several activations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In overcomplete toy MLPs, neurons aligned in weight space to one cluster's features still fire substantially on other clusters. Mixed firing then arises without capacity pressure, via shared input coordinates.

record.problems: The evidence concerns synthetic, well-separated Gaussian-mixture regression and an operational cluster-based monosemanticity score, not natural semantic concepts or canonical polysemantic neurons. Monosemanticity is reported among neurons meeting the study's specialization criterion, rather than as a direct count of polysemantic neurons across the entire network.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant monosemanticity results from Tables 1–3 were left out. Results on specialization alignment, predictive MSE, and MLP-gated predictors were excluded because they do not themselves measure the semantic activation behavior named in the tested version.

untested.parts: SoLU, convnets, transformer or language models, and regularization as a factor. No intervention is aimed at lowering polysemanticity. Only one-hidden-layer synthetic MLPs with ReLU, GELU, ReGLU and SwiGLU are tested.
Superposition or capacity pressure is not manipulated.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
The Mj threshold and scoring are not varied for monosemanticity. Only the specialization threshold (0.7 vs 0.9) is varied, in Table 6.

missing.what: Test MSE per activation in the same models whose monosemanticity is reported. This bears on V5's 'without large performance loss' (e.g., ReGLU 0.0119 vs ReLU 0.0544 test MSE).
Share of all active neurons that are specialized, per activation. It is needed to convert the Mj > 1/2 share into a share over all neurons.

record.verdict_notes: This is a toy setting: 'features' are synthetic Gaussian clusters, not semantic concepts, so the link to V5 is indirect. Monosemanticity is measured only among neurons with Sj ≥ 0.9. Active-neuron counts differ about tenfold across activations, which complicates comparing shares. Not an original source. Tranche changed from the reader's T2 to T3 (new setting).

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers and responses to unrelated visual inputs are not studied.
Transformer language models, tokens, and language contexts are not studied.
The study does not test whether neuron mixing is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
The study does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or noise when capacity is sufficient.

The study compares ReLU, GELU, ReGLU, and SwiGLU in one-hidden-layer synthetic MLPs. It does not test SoLU, modern convnets, or whether lowering polysemanticity can be done without a large performance loss.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their apparently unrelated responses share a semantic feature such as pose.
The study does not vary activation-range slices or explanation-scoring methods to test measurement dependence.

relationships.condition: One-hidden-layer width-4096 MLPs on synthetic clustered regression, across the three experiments (Tables 1–3)
relationships.reason: Cluster-selectivity of specialized neurons changes strongly with activation. ReGLU is highest (95.6–100% with Mj > 1/2; T1-R6, T2-R6, T3-R6) versus GELU 45.7–79.8% (T1-R4, T2-R4, T3-R4). ReGLU also has lower test MSE than ReLU/GELU (Table 4, not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: ReGLU gave the highest cluster-selectivity, 95.6–100% with Mj > 1/2, against 45.7–79.8% for GELU, and ReGLU also had lower test MSE than ReLU and GELU.

source_check.condition: One-hidden-layer width-4096 MLPs on synthetic clustered regression, across the three experiments (Tables 1–3)
source_check.reason: Share with Mj > 1/2 varies 45.7-100% by activation. ReGLU is top in Tables 1 and 3, but in Table 2 ReLU 99.50 >= ReGLU 99.22 (verdict says ReGLU highest). ReGLU test MSE 0.0119 vs ReLU 0.0544 and GELU 0.0235 (Table 4).

relationships.condition: Ranking across activations depends on data geometry
relationships.reason: ReLU is mid-ranked in the axis-aligned setting (65.7%, T1-R2) but near-perfect in the non-orthogonal and multi-index settings (99.5–99.8%, T2-R2, T3-R2). SwiGLU falls below ReLU there (68.9%, 56.7%; T2-R8, T3-R8). So activation effects are not a fixed ordering.
relationships.display_finding: ReLU ranked mid-table in the axis-aligned setting (65.7%) but was near-perfect in the non-orthogonal and multi-index settings (99.5–99.8%), where SwiGLU fell below it (68.9% and 56.7%).

relation.reason: Its own Tables 1-3 compare neuron selectivity across activations, which bears on V5.

tranche.reason: New synthetic clustered-regression setting with its own selectivity measure (Mj); the result bears on V5 as a toy analogue. The reader's T2 is less apt because the study does not aim at the polysemanticity question.

source_check.notes: Percentages are over specialized neurons only, and the specialized share differs widely (Table 1: ReLU 15.71% of 3879 active vs GELU 77.66% of 431), so cross-activation comparison of the share is confounded. Toy analogue of monosemanticity (cluster selectivity), not interpretability on real models. In Table 4, SwiGLU has the lowest test MSE (0.00510) despite lower selectivity than ReGLU.

statements.problem: This study's numbers match Table 1 (95.57, 71.80, 65.74, 45.74 with these SDs) and Tables 1-3 ranges (ReGLU 95.57-100.00, GELU 45.74-79.84). Table 4 is legible and confirms lower ReGLU test MSE (0.01185 vs ReLU 0.05436, GELU 0.02349), though only for the axis-aligned K=25 experiment. No code link in text; SD over 3 seeds confirmed.

For this study: ReLU 65.74% (Table 1) vs 99.50% (Table 2) and 99.80% (Table 3); SwiGLU 68.86% and 56.67% fall below ReLU in Tables 2-3, while SwiGLU 71.80% > ReLU 65.74% in Table 1. Matches. The settings also differ in K (25 vs 50) and d (60 vs 40), which 'data regime' covers.
Correct for this study: no SoLU; only ReLU, GELU, ReGLU and SwiGLU are varied.
Correct: this study reports the share with Mj > 1/2 over specialized neurons (Sj >= 0.9) only.

ReLU 65.74% (axis-aligned) vs 99.50% (non-orthogonal) correct. The ranking change itself is shown by SwiGLU vs ReLU flipping, which the ReLU numbers imply only in part, but the statement is not wrong.
Only the mention of this study (synthetic MLPs, group other than the original's: Abedsoltan, Boix-Adsera, Kalogiannis, Belkin) is checkable; it is right.
Width 4096, K = 25 (Exp 3.1) and 50 (Exp 3.2-3.3) right; GELU 45.74% (Table 1) and SwiGLU 56.67% (Table 3) right.
